source_refs.note: Topic 20.3.1 with Quick Checks 20.4 to 20.6, answered (PDF 65-68); the mechanisms are redrawn. The book says the sigma complex is 'deprotonated by AlCl4-' in bromination; it is [AlBr4]-. The learning outcomes' 'neutronium ion' is the nitronium ion. Answers need review.

blocks.text: Whatever the electrophile, electrophilic aromatic substitution happens in three main steps.

items: Generation of the electrophile: the electrophile, a positive ion or the positive end of a polar molecule, usually cannot simply be added; it is made in the reaction mixture (in situ) from suitable reagents.

Electrophilic attack: pi electrons of the ring attack the electrophile, forming a sigma bond between one ring carbon and the electrophile. This breaks the aromaticity: only four pi electrons remain, and a positive charge is spread over the other five carbons. This intermediate is the sigma complex (arenium ion).
Restoration of aromaticity: a base (counter-ion) removes the H from the sp3 carbon. The C-H bond breaks heterolytically, its electrons go back into the pi system, and the delocalisation is restored.

blocks.text: Benzene reacts with chlorine or bromine only in the presence of a Lewis acid, such as aluminium chloride (AlCl3), iron(III) chloride (FeCl3) or iron(III) bromide (FeBr3), which coordinates to the halogen and generates a strong electrophile. For bromination: C6H6 + Br2 -> C6H5Br + HBr (anhydrous AlBr3).

items: Br2 + AlBr3 -> Br+ + [AlBr4]-: the Lewis acid polarises Br2 and forms the electrophile.
Br+ attacks the ring, giving the sigma complex.
[AlBr4]- removes H+ from the sigma complex: bromobenzene, HBr and AlBr3 (the catalyst) are formed.

blocks.alt: Top: the general mechanism, benzene attacked by E+ to give a sigma complex (a ring with a horseshoe of positive charge and an sp3 carbon bearing H and E), which loses H+ to give the substituted ring. Bottom: Br-Br + AlBr3 gives Br+ + [AlBr4]-; Br+ attacks benzene; [AlBr4]- removes H+, giving bromobenzene + HBr + AlBr3.
blocks.caption: Electrophilic aromatic substitution and the bromination of benzene (original mechanisms after the book's diagrams).
blocks.long_description: The slow step is the attack by the electrophile, which forms the sigma complex and breaks the aromatic ring. In the fast step the ring loses a proton and becomes aromatic again. In bromination the Lewis acid AlBr3 makes the Br+ electrophile and is given back at the end, so it is a catalyst.

blocks.text: Chlorination is the same, with FeCl3 or AlCl3 as the Lewis acid generating Cl+.
A nitro group is put on benzene with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids: C6H6 + HNO3 -> C6H5NO2 + H2O (conc. H2SO4).

items: Formation of the electrophile: H2SO4 + HNO3 <=> NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O. The nitronium ion NO2+ is the electrophile.
Attack: a pair of electrons from the ring bonds to NO2+, forming the sigma complex and losing the aromaticity.
The C-H bond of the substituted carbon breaks and its electrons return to the pi system, restoring the ring: nitrobenzene forms.
Regeneration of the catalyst: HSO4- + H+ -> H2SO4.

blocks.alt: Step 1: HNO3 + H2SO4 gives NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O. Steps 2 and 3: NO2+ attacks benzene, giving a sigma complex with H and NO2 on one carbon, which loses H+ to give nitrobenzene; H+ + HSO4- re-forms H2SO4. Overall C6H6 + HNO3 gives C6H5NO2 + H2O with conc. H2SO4 below about 50 C.
blocks.caption: The nitration of benzene (original mechanism after the book's diagram).
blocks.long_description: Sulphuric acid, the stronger acid, protonates nitric acid, which then loses water to give the nitronium ion. NO2+ is attacked by the ring, and the sigma complex loses a proton. The proton combines with HSO4- to re-form sulphuric acid, so sulphuric acid acts as a catalyst and is not written in the overall equation.

blocks.text: At higher temperatures more than one nitro group can enter the ring; some 1,3-dinitrobenzene forms even at 50 C: C6H5NO2 + HNO3 -> 1,3-C6H4(NO2)2 + H2O.

In Friedel-Crafts alkylation an alkyl group is substituted into the benzene ring; in Friedel-Crafts acylation an acyl group, R-C=O (an alkyl group attached to a carbonyl group), is substituted, in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst.

items: Alkylation: C6H6 + CH3CH2Cl -> C6H5CH2CH3 (ethylbenzene) + HCl (AlCl3 catalyst, heat).
Acylation: C6H6 + CH3CH2COCl -> C6H5COCH2CH3 + HCl (AlCl3 catalyst, heat).

Alkylation (three steps): the Lewis acid AlCl3 reacts with the alkyl halide to form a carbocation, the electrophile, e.g. (CH3)3C-Cl + AlCl3 -> (CH3)3C+ + [AlCl4]- (a tertiary carbocation); the pi electrons of the ring attack the carbocation, forming an arenium ion; the intermediate loses a proton, restoring the aromaticity, and the proton forms HCl, regenerating AlCl3.

Acylation: AlCl3 forms a complex with the acyl halide, which loses a halide ion to give an acylium ion, RCO+; the ring's pi electrons attack the acylium ion; the intermediate is deprotonated, restoring the ring, forming HCl and regenerating AlCl3. The product is an aryl ketone.

blocks.alt: Top: (CH3)3C-Cl + AlCl3 gives the tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+ + [AlCl4]-; it attacks benzene to give a sigma complex, and [AlCl4]- removes H+ to give tert-butylbenzene + HCl + AlCl3. Bottom: R-COCl + AlCl3 gives the acylium ion R-C+=O + [AlCl4]-; it attacks benzene and the sigma complex loses H+, giving the aryl ketone C6H5COR + HCl + AlCl3.
blocks.caption: Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation (original mechanisms after the book's diagrams).
blocks.long_description: In both reactions AlCl3 takes the chlorine from the organic halide and leaves a carbon electrophile: a carbocation for alkylation and an acylium ion for acylation. The ring attacks this electrophile, and the [AlCl4]- ion takes back a proton, giving HCl and returning the AlCl3 catalyst.

blocks.prompt: Write the mechanism for the reaction of benzene with chlorine using AlCl3 as catalyst.
blocks.explanation: Cl2 + AlCl3 -> Cl+ + [AlCl4]-; Cl+ attacks the ring, giving the sigma complex; [AlCl4]- removes H+, giving chlorobenzene + HCl + AlCl3.

blocks.prompt: Show how the electrophile is made in nitration. Which acid acts as an acid and which as a base?
blocks.explanation: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4- (simplified: H2SO4 + HNO3 -> NO2+ + HSO4- + H2O). Sulphuric acid is the acid (proton donor); nitric acid accepts the proton and acts as a base.

blocks.prompt: Write the reaction of methylbenzene with bromine in the presence of AlBr3.
blocks.explanation: Ring substitution at positions 2 and 4: C6H5CH3 + Br2 -> 2-bromomethylbenzene and 4-bromomethylbenzene (a mixture) + HBr.

blocks.prompt: How does bromine react with benzene and with phenol?
blocks.explanation: Both are electrophilic substitutions. Benzene needs liquid bromine and a Lewis acid catalyst (FeBr3 or AlBr3) and gives bromobenzene + HBr. Phenol's OH group activates the ring so strongly that bromine water reacts at room temperature without a catalyst, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol + 3HBr.

blocks.prompt: How does bromine react with benzene and with ethylbenzene?
blocks.explanation: With a Lewis acid catalyst in the dark both undergo ring substitution: benzene gives bromobenzene; ethylbenzene reacts faster (the ethyl group activates the ring) giving 2- and 4-bromoethylbenzene. In UV light without a catalyst, ethylbenzene instead undergoes free-radical substitution in the side chain, mainly at the CH2 next to the ring, giving (1-bromoethyl)benzene; benzene's ring is not substituted this way.

blocks.prompt: Which is easier to make by a Friedel-Crafts reaction, 1,1-dimethylethylbenzene or methylbenzene? Explain.
blocks.explanation: 1,1-dimethylethylbenzene (tert-butylbenzene): its electrophile is the tertiary carbocation (CH3)3C+, which is stabilised by three alkyl groups, whereas methylbenzene would need the very unstable methyl cation CH3+.

items: Three steps: make E+, attack (sigma complex), lose H+.
Halogenation (Br2/AlBr3), nitration (NO2+ from HNO3 + H2SO4), Friedel-Crafts (R+ or RCO+ from AlCl3).
The Lewis acid or H2SO4 is regenerated: a catalyst.
